answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Bruce Lee ever used this line. As Quote Investigator ↗ documents, the complete four-part “knows / knows not” saying was already printed as an “Arabic proverb” in The Globe of Toronto in 1885 — decades before Lee was born in 1940. Lee’s name was only attached to it much later, appearing on Goodreads by 2017.

source.excerpt: He who knows not, and knows not he knows not. He is a fool; shun him. He who knows not, and knows he knows not. He is simple; teach him. He who knows, and knows not he knows. He is asleep; wake him. He who knows, and knows he knows. He is wise; follow him.
trail: A three-part precursor — “if a man does not know, and does not know that he does not know” — appears as an “Oriental maxim” by 1866, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The complete four-part version was printed as an “Arabic proverb” in The Globe of Toronto in 1885, and appeared in Isabel Burton’s 1893 biography of Richard Francis Burton as an “Arab Proverb,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence that Bruce Lee… employed this expression”; his name appears attached to it only by 2017 on Goodreads ↗, where it is also filed under “Persian Proverb.”
source.excerptNote: The 1885 The Globe (Toronto) text, printed as an “Arabic proverb.” The version circulated under Bruce Lee’s name is a lightly re-punctuated form of this same saying.

author.name: An anonymous proverb
author.heading: A wandering proverb with no single author
author.metaLine: Full four-part English version in print by 1885 · variously called an Arabic, Persian & Chinese proverb
author.bio: This is a traditional proverb, not a line from any identified writer. Its English form built up over the 1800s: a three-part “Oriental maxim” circulated by 1866, and the complete four-part “knows / knows not” ladder appeared as an “Arabic proverb” by 1885. Over the years it has been labelled Arabic, Persian, Chinese and Confucian, and — most recently and just as baselessly — pinned on Bruce Lee.

misattribution.heading: A proverb with many false owners
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “floating” proverb: because no one can name its true author, it gets re-assigned to whoever sounds plausible. Bruce Lee is only the latest name attached to it.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence that Bruce Lee… employed this expression.” His name appears attached to it only by 2017, on Goodreads — decades after his death and a century after the saying was already in print.

items.who: Confucius, Lady Isabel Burton, and “Persian / Chinese proverb”
items.why: The same lines circulate under many labels — Arabic, Persian, and Chinese proverb, and even Confucius — per Quote Investigator ↗. None is documented as the original source; they reflect the saying’s wandering, anonymous history.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: it is an anonymous proverb whose full English form was in print by 1885, not a Bruce Lee quotation, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it gets pinned on Bruce Lee
lead: Bruce Lee (1940–1973) is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: crisp, aphoristic wisdom about self-mastery gets attached to his name because it sounds like him. This four-part saying about knowing and not-knowing fits that mold perfectly — but it predates him by more than half a century.

The saying is genuinely old and genuinely anonymous. What the record shows is a proverb that drifted across cultures and attributions for over a century before Lee’s name was ever attached to it around 2017.
context.pull: In print as an “Arabic proverb” in 1885 — before Bruce Lee was born.
